_about: Behavioral answers with the scores a careful human reviewer would give. Ranges are [min, max] on the 1-4 rubric; stars are the overall 1-5. Written for this project; any similarity to real people is accidental.

items.question: Tell me about a time you had a conflict with a teammate.
items.look_for: How they handled disagreement: listened, used evidence, kept the relationship.
items.situation: In my junior-year software engineering course, our four-person team had three weeks to ship a course-scheduling app for 300 students. Our frontend lead wanted to drop the search feature to save time; I owned the backend and thought search was the main reason students would use it.
items.task: Settle it fast without splitting the team, because the TA graded us partly on teamwork.
items.action: I asked him for 20 minutes to look at data together. I pulled the survey we'd run in week one: 41 of 58 students listed search as their top need. I offered to build the search endpoint myself over the weekend and proposed cutting the dark mode feature instead, which he had planned. We agreed to check progress on Monday and drop search if it wasn't working by then.
items.result: Search worked by Monday, we shipped on time, and in the class demo 70% of test users used search first. We got 96/100 and the TA singled out how we resolved scope.
items.reflection: I learned to bring data and a concrete offer to a disagreement instead of arguing opinions. In my internship this summer I did the same when my manager and I disagreed on test coverage.

items.question: Tell me about a time you had a conflict with a teammate.
items.look_for: How they handled disagreement: listened, used evidence, kept the relationship.
items.situation: We had a group project and there was a disagreement.
items.task: We needed to finish the project.
items.action: We talked about it as a team and we found a compromise that worked for everyone.
items.result: It went well and we finished.
items.reflection: I learned that communication is important.

items.question: Tell me about a time you took initiative.
items.look_for: Something they started without being asked, and what came of it.
items.situation: At my part-time job at the campus library, students waited up to 25 minutes at the help desk during finals week because the same five questions came up again and again.
items.task: Nobody asked me to, but I wanted to cut the wait.
items.action: I logged every question for two shifts, found that 60% were about printing and room booking, wrote a one-page FAQ with screenshots, and convinced my supervisor to put QR codes to it on every table. I also trained two other student workers to point people to it.
items.result: Average wait during the next finals week dropped to under 8 minutes, and the library kept the FAQ for the next year.

items.question: Tell me about a time you failed.
items.look_for: Owning a real failure, what they did about it, and what they learned.
items.situation: Last spring I led the finance committee of our investment club and was responsible for the pitch for our annual stock competition.
items.task: Deliver a pitch on a mid-cap retailer.
items.action: I built the DCF alone the night before and didn't ask anyone to check it. During the pitch a judge found that I had double-counted capex, which changed our target price completely. I owned the mistake on the spot, then rebuilt the model with two members the following week and set up a rule that every model gets a second checker.
items.result: We didn't place that year, but things got better afterwards.
items.reflection: I learned that speed without review is a false saving. Since then I always schedule a review a day before any deadline, and I did that for every model in my internship.

items.question: Tell me about a time you led a team.
items.look_for: Leading others: setting direction, motivating, handling problems.
items.situation: Last summer I wanted to learn Python on my own.
items.action: I studied every evening for six weeks and built a small web scraper for stock prices.
items.result: I finished the course and the scraper works.
items.reflection: I learned I can teach myself.

items.question: 请讲一次你在团队中发挥关键作用的经历。
items.look_for: Teamwork: their specific role and how the team succeeded because of it.
items.situation: 大二时我参加了学校的数学建模竞赛，三人一组，72小时内完成一篇关于共享单车调度的论文。比赛第二天，我们的模型在大数据量下跑不出结果，离截止只剩30小时。
items.task: 我负责编程，需要让模型在截止前跑完。
items.action: 我先用小样本找出瓶颈是距离矩阵的重复计算，然后改用KD树做最近邻搜索，又把整数规划拆成按区域的子问题并行求解。同时我每4小时给队友同步一次结果，让他们边写论文边更新图表。
items.result: 运行时间从超过6小时降到25分钟，我们按时提交并获得省级一等奖（全省前5%）。
items.reflection: 我学到遇到卡点先量化瓶颈再动手。后来做课程项目时我都会先做性能分析，而不是直接重写代码。

items.question: Tell me about your biggest accomplishment.

items.action: I worked really hard and was very proactive.

items.question: Tell me about a time you worked under a tight deadline.
items.look_for: Prioritizing and delivering under time pressure.
items.situation: In my accounting class, our group's case report was due in two days and one member got sick, so we were missing the cash flow section.
items.task: Make sure the report was complete.
items.action: I took over the cash flow statement and stayed up late to finish it.
items.result: We submitted the report on time.
items.reflection: I learned to stay calm under pressure.

items.question: Tell me about a project you're proud of.
items.look_for: A project they drove, what they built or did, and the impact.
items.situation: I'm building an app that helps international students find part-time jobs on campus, because my friends kept missing postings.
items.task: Build the first version this semester.
items.action: I designed the database, wrote a scraper for the campus job board, and built the React front end. I interviewed 12 international students to decide which filters matter, and added a visa-status filter because 9 of them asked for it.
items.reflection: Talking to users first changed what I built.

items.question: Tell me about a time you had to learn something quickly.
items.look_for: Learning fast under pressure and applying it.
items.situation: So this was during my sophomore summer, I had an internship at a small private equity firm, it was only six people, and honestly I didn't really know much about private equity at the time, I had taken one finance class. On my second day the associate told me we had a management meeting with a portfolio company in four days and they needed an LBO model for an add-on acquisition and I would be building the first version.
items.task: Build a working LBO model in four days without having built one before.
items.action: I spent the first evening going through two LBO training guides and rebuilt their example model from scratch. The next day I asked the associate for 15 minutes to confirm the structure he wanted: senior debt, a seller note, and a 5-year hold. I built the model, then tested it by changing each assumption to see if the outputs moved the right way, and found that my debt schedule wasn't sweeping excess cash, which I fixed. I sent it a day early so he had time to review.
items.result: He used my model in the meeting with only minor changes, and the firm used my debt schedule template for the next two deals.
items.reflection: I learned to rebuild a known-good example before building my own, and to stress-test outputs instead of trusting them. I now do the same with every new kind of model.

items.question: Tell me about yourself.
items.look_for: A short, tailored pitch: who you are, what you've done, why this role.
items.answer: I'm a junior at the University of Illinois studying finance and computer science, and I'm looking for a private equity internship. Last summer I interned at a six-person search fund, where I screened 140 small businesses and built the model for one we sent an LOI to. On campus I run the valuation team of our investment club, where I teach 20 new members to build DCFs. I'm drawn to small PE because I liked seeing one company up close, and I want to keep doing the analysis that decides whether a deal happens.

items.question: Tell me about yourself.
items.look_for: A short, tailored pitch: who you are, what you've done, why this role.
items.answer: I am a hardworking and passionate student who loves challenges. I am a team player and a fast learner, and I am very interested in finance. I believe I would be a great fit for your company.

items.question: What is your greatest weakness?
items.look_for: A real weakness, honest, with what they're doing about it.
items.answer: My greatest weakness is that I'm a perfectionist. I care too much about my work.

items.question: What is your greatest weakness?
items.look_for: A real weakness, honest, with what they're doing about it.
items.answer: I used to avoid speaking up in meetings when I wasn't sure I was right. In my first internship I noticed a formula error in a client deck but waited a day to mention it, and my manager found it right before it was sent. Since then I've made a rule to raise anything I'm 70% sure about, framed as a question. This semester I've also joined Toastmasters and given four speeches, and my manager at my current job told me I now flag issues earlier than most of the team.

items.question: Why investment banking?
items.look_for: Specific, personal reasons that show they know what the job is.
items.answer: Three reasons. First, I like transactions: in my internship at a 12-person sell-side boutique I helped with the teaser and buyer list for a $40M HVAC company sale, and seeing it close was the most energizing work I've done. Second, the learning curve: I want to build models and read companies faster than in any other job, and the analysts I've spoken with at your firm described doing exactly that on middle-market deals. Third, I want to advise founders, because my parents sold their small business and I saw how much a good advisor mattered.

items.question: Why do you want to work in data science?
items.look_for: Specific reasons and evidence of interest.
items.answer: Well, it's kind of a long story, I first got into computers when I was young, I played a lot of games, and then in high school I did some coding but not much, and then in college I took statistics, which was fine, and also some economics, and I think data is the future, everyone says so, and also the salaries are good, and my cousin works at a tech company and he likes it, so I think it would be good, and I like solving problems I guess.
